lead: Surveying finds the relative positions of points on or near the earth and draws them on a map or plan. It exists because a road, a plot boundary or a dam must be placed in correct relation to everything around it. Surveys are classified by purpose, by instrument, and by whether the earth’s curvature is included. This chapter fixes the vocabulary and the two working principles used in every later survey.

blocks.text: Surveying is the art and science of determining the relative positions of points on or near the surface of the earth, and of representing them on a map or plan at a chosen scale. The object is not only to measure a distance but to fix a point in relation to a known framework.

Two principles govern field work. First, work from the whole to the part. Establish a broad, accurate control network first—a set of well-fixed reference points—then fill in details from that control. Errors stay small and local instead of accumulating across the site. Second, fix a new point by at least two independent measurements. One distance from one known point places the new point on a circle around that point. A second distance from another known point cuts that circle at two points; a rough sketch of the site, or a third measurement, decides which of the two is the real point. Two angles from two known points also fix it. Surveyors call fixing by distances trilateration. A single measurement is never enough for position.
Direct distance work is covered in chain and tape surveying and EDM.
Classification by purpose answers a simple question: what is the survey for?

items: Topographic surveying maps natural and man-made features and the relief of the ground. It supports route selection, drainage and site planning; the map is read with map scales and topographic sheets.
Cadastral surveying fixes land parcel boundaries, ownership and area. Revenue offices use it for land records and taxation.
Engineering surveying supplies design data and sets out works such as roads, bridges and pipelines during construction.
Control surveying builds the accurate framework of points on which other surveys depend.
Hydrographic surveying maps water bodies, depths and shores for navigation, dredging and flood work.
Astronomical surveying determines latitude, longitude or azimuth from stars; it is now rare in routine work but explains older control.

blocks.text: A project can need several classes at once. A highway may start with control, use topographic survey for alignment, cadastral survey for land, and engineering survey for setting out.

The instrument names the main quantity measured or the main tool used. The name also hints at what the survey can deliver: distances alone, bearings alone, angles with distances, or coordinates directly.

items: Chain or tape surveying measures distances directly and builds a framework of lines and offsets; it cannot measure angles well.
Compass surveying measures magnetic bearings of lines, so it handles traverses where angles are needed but precision is moderate.
Theodolite surveying measures horizontal and vertical angles precisely. It is the base of triangulation and tacheometry.
Total station surveying combines an electronic distance meter with angle measurement and computes coordinates in the field.
GNSS surveying (Global Navigation Satellite System) uses satellite signals to give position; it is fast for control and detail where sky view is open.

blocks.text: Modern classes such as UAV (drone) and LiDAR (laser scanning) surveying are now named separately; their working belongs to Unit 5, Modern Surveying: Total Station and GNSS. A surveyor chooses the simplest instrument that meets the required precision.
This split depends on one question: does the curvature of the earth matter at the precision you need?

In plane surveying, the earth is treated as flat. Horizontal distances and angles are taken on a plane, and ordinary plane geometry is used. This is valid for most engineering works: a building site, a town map, a canal alignment. A common working limit is an area up to about 250 km². It is a guide, not a law; the decision also depends on the precision required and the length of individual sights.

In geodetic surveying, the curvature is included. The earth is represented by a spheroid, a flattened ellipsoid that approximates the earth, and positions are computed on that curved surface. This is needed for large areas, long baselines, national control and precise maps. A 600 km baseline is geodetic work. Plane formulas would bend the answer by many metres.
For a sight of length d, the earth’s curvature lifts the far point by about:

blocks.where: c is the curvature correction in the same unit as d; d is the horizontal sight length; R is the mean earth radius, about 6371 km.

blocks.text: At d = 10 km, c is about 7.85 m, which no engineer can ignore. Datum details are in datums and coordinate systems.

examples.question: A town area is 12 km × 8 km. (a) Is a plane survey acceptable? (b) For a 600 km long geodetic baseline, which survey is needed? (c) Estimate the curvature correction for a 10 km sight with R = 6371 km.
steps: Area = 12 × 8 = 96 km². 96 km² is below the working guide of about 250 km², so plane surveying is acceptable for the town map.
600 km is far beyond the plane limit and is a long baseline; geodetic surveying is needed.
examples.answer: The town may be surveyed as a plane survey (96 km²); the 600 km baseline needs geodetic surveying; and the 10 km curvature correction is about 7.85 m.
examples.check:
area = 12 * 8
print(float(area))
d = 10000.0
R = 6371000.0
c = d * d / (2 * R)
print(round(c, 2))

traps: Reversing the first principle: work from the whole to the part, not from the part to the whole. Starting with detail makes errors grow.
Treating the 250 km² limit as a legal rule. It is a guide; precision and sight length decide.
Mixing topographic and cadastral: topographic shows features and relief; cadastral shows parcel boundaries and ownership.
Putting d and R in different units in c = d²/(2R). Convert both to metres, or both to kilometres, before dividing.
Calling any large survey geodetic without checking curvature and precision; and calling any small survey plane when a long precise sight may still need curvature.

quiz.a: Surveying determines relative positions of points on or near the earth and represents them on a map or plan at a chosen scale.

quiz.q: Why is a point fixed by at least two independent measurements?
quiz.a: One measurement leaves a locus of possible positions; a second independent measurement intersects that locus and narrows the position to one or two candidates, and a sketch or a third measurement settles which one it is.

quiz.q: A rectangular site is 15 km × 10 km. Find its area and state whether plane surveying is acceptable by the usual guide.
quiz.a: Area = 15 × 10 = 150 km²; 150 km² is below 250 km², so plane surveying is acceptable.

quiz.q: Find the curvature correction for a 6 km sight with R = 6371 km.
A survey covers only 40 km² but must connect points 30 km apart to centimetre precision. Is plane surveying automatically acceptable? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The area guide is not the only test. Long precise sights need a curvature check; a 30 km sight gives c ≈ 70.6 m, so geodetic methods or curvature corrections are needed.

quiz.q: Name any four purposes used to classify surveys.
quiz.a: Topographic, cadastral, engineering and control (also hydrographic and astronomical).

quiz.q: Give one difference between plane and geodetic surveying.
quiz.a: Plane surveying treats the earth as flat and ignores curvature; geodetic surveying includes curvature and uses a spheroid for large areas or long baselines.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, control is now computed by least-squares network adjustment, and detail is captured with total stations, GNSS rovers, UAV photogrammetry or LiDAR. Cadastral records in India increasingly link parcel geometry to digital maps and coordinate databases. Surveyors still decide plane or geodetic by computing curvature and propagation of error, not by area alone.
